primary_reviews.rationale: This was the designated focus test and the outcome is mixed: I would keep the span, but the record cannot stand as written. Two things are wrong with it. First, the stated ground is factually inaccurate. The draft describes five prohibitions 'each opening its own bare לֹא-clause' forming 'a formally uniform register'. In the Hebrew only 5:17 is bare -- לֹא תִּרְצָח. The next four are waw-coordinated: וְלֹא תִּנְאָף, וְלֹא תִּגְנֹב, וְלֹא תַעֲנֶה, וְלֹא תַחְמֹד. And the register is not uniform: vv.17-19 run two words each, while v.21 runs to seventeen and contains a second internal prohibition, וְלֹא תִתְאַוֶּה, with a six-item enumeration. 'Unelaborated' is simply false of the last verse. Second, and more serious, the draft never discloses that both available paragraphing witnesses split what it joins. The OSHB XML carries a setumah after each of 5:17, 5:18, 5:19 and 5:20, and two after 5:21 (all verified present) -- the densest paragraphing in this book. WEB's editorial paragraphing likewise breaks at every one of those verses. The irony is that the argument that actually saves the span is the one the draft transcribed but did not use: the waw-chain grammatically coordinates vv.18-21 to v.17 as one series, which is precisely the Deuteronomic feature that distinguishes this Decalogue from the asyndetic Exodus recension. That is a text signal, it drives, and it outranks weak setumot and inadmissible editorial marks. Keep the boundary; rebuild the warrant.

primary_reviews.rationale: This genuinely is the closest call in the Decalogue, and the evidence pulls in both directions strongly enough that I cannot resolve it to a confident verdict either way. Against the merge: WEB gives each of the five commands its own separate paragraph mark (a break before v.17, before v.18, before v.19, before v.20, and before v.21 individually), the single most granular stretch of paragraphing anywhere in the chapter, and each command addresses a genuinely independent legal category elsewhere treated separately in Torah casuistic law (killing, sexual fidelity, property, testimony, desire). For the merge: all five share one continuous bare-apodictic register with no rationale or motive clause attached to any of them, unlike every other command in the chapter, and that formal homogeneity — not topical similarity — is the operative literary-unity criterion; the per-verse WEB paragraphing looks best explained as a presentational or catechetical convention (WEB applies the identical per-command paragraphing to the first table too, at v.7 and v.11, where the draft correctly does not treat that formatting as decisive, since those commands differ in mood and each carries its own rationale). The draft's own rejected alternative candidly flags this as 'the single most contestable granularity call' without resolving it, and I don't think ten verses on either side settles it either — a reasonable form-critical reviewer could land on five decisions here just as easily as one.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: This is the designated focus test and all three challenge rows on it point at the same underlying problem from different angles. The drafted rationale's central claim -- that all five commands each open their own bare לֹא-clause in a formally uniform register -- does not survive a verbatim check: only 5:17 is asyndetic; 5:18-21 are all waw-coordinated, and 5:21 alone runs to a second internal prohibition plus a six-item enumeration, nothing like the two-word terseness of 5:17. That register claim is simply wrong as written, which is what OL-1 argues. OL-2 is also right that the record omits the countervailing Masoretic witness entirely: samekh sites fall after every one of 5:17 through 5:21, the densest paragraphing anywhere in this book, and WEB independently paragraphs each command too, none of it disclosed in boundary_evidence_refs. Where I land: the waw-chain OL proposes as the real warrant -- that the coordination binds 18-21 back to 17 as one series, a feature this Decalogue has and the asyndetic Exodus recension does not -- is a genuine text signal and not marker-only, and I would keep the span on that ground. But five setumot dividing exactly what the coordination chain is being asked to unify is a real, not merely absent, countervailing signal even at weak class, and LF's insufficient_evidence flag is the honest response to that tension rather than a cop-out. I would retain the span as a candidate at low-to-frontier confidence, with the warrant rebuilt on coordination syntax rather than a uniform register the text does not have, and the setumah pattern disclosed rather than suppressed.

primary_reviews.rationale: Closing edge holds. 11:7 seals the retrospective with כִּ֤י עֵֽינֵיכֶם֙ הָֽרֹאֹ֔ת אֶת כָּל מַעֲשֵׂ֥ה יְהוָ֖ה הַגָּדֹ֑ל, and 11:8 restarts on the full charge-formula וּשְׁמַרְתֶּם֙ אֶת כָּל הַמִּצְוָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֛ר אָנֹכִ֥י מְצַוְּךָ֖ הַיּ֑וֹם. The opening edge is where this decision goes wrong. Verse 1 is uniformly second masculine singular (וְאָ֣הַבְתָּ֔ and וְשָׁמַרְתָּ֣, both Vqq2ms) and re-runs, verb for verb, the infinitive chain of 10:12-13 (וּלְאַהֲבָ֣ה אֹת֔וֹ ... לִשְׁמֹ֞ר אֶת מִצְוֺ֤ת יְהוָה֙). WLC agrees to the extent that it records no division at 10:22|11:1 at all: its paragraph runs from the petuchah after 10:11 to the setumah after 11:9. Read on its own signals, 11:1 is the summarizing close of the 10:12-22 charge rather than the head of an Exodus retrospective.

primary_reviews.rationale: This is the crosswalk-offset decision, and the draft reaches the right span for the wrong reason. Decisive datum the draft never cites: WLC places a PETUCHAH after MT 13:1 — i.e. after the very verse WEB numbers 12:32 — with no division anywhere between the setumah after 12:28 and that petuchah. The manuscript therefore delimits exactly MT 12:29-13:1 = WEB 12:29-32 as one paragraph, and WEB's own editorial paragraphing independently agrees (a break before 12:29, none before 12:32). Second, the add-nothing verse reuses the same שמר-frame that had just closed the previous paragraph at 12:28 (שְׁמֹר וְשָׁמַעְתָּ ... אֲשֶׁר אָנֹכִי מְצַוֶּךָּ / אֵת כָּל הַדָּבָר אֲשֶׁר אָנֹכִי מְצַוֶּה אֶתְכֶם אֹתוֹ תִשְׁמְרוּ לַעֲשׂוֹת), and in both places the frame is followed immediately by a divider: the formula is functioning as a closing device twice in a row. Third, MT 13:2 begins a plain casuistic protasis (כִּי יָקוּם בְּקִרְבְּךָ), which needs no heading. Two corrections. (a) The draft's stated ground — that הַדָּבָר means 'this word' and points back — is not what the Hebrew says: the noun is definite by virtue of its own following relative clause and there is no הַזֶּה, so it is cataphoric; compare 4:2, where the identical canon formula is prospective and uniformly plural (תֹסִפוּ / תִגְרְעוּ). (b) The honest counter-signal, which the draft also misses, is the Numeruswechsel: 12:28-31 is second-singular throughout, MT 13:1 opens plural (אֶתְכֶם, תִשְׁמְרוּ) and ends singular (תֹסֵף, תִגְרַע), and MT 13:2 is singular. The plural head detaches the verse from what precedes; the singular tail leans forward. That is real, but it is one internal alternation against a petuchah plus a twice-used closing frame, so the span holds. Low confidence understates the record; medium is warranted. Finally, this decision is the only one in the offset zone with no Hebrew quotation of the disputed verse at all — the oshb ref points to the span's opening verse instead.

primary_reviews.rationale: This is the flagged 12:32/13:1 offset, and it is a genuine crux rather than a settled call in either direction. For WEB's placement (closing centralization law): “this word/thing” (הַדָּבָר) carries the definite article, naturally referring back to the legislative complex just given rather than introducing new content, and 13:1's own casuistic protasis (“If a prophet or a dreamer of dreams arises among you”) is fully self-sufficient as a case-opening, needing no lead-in formula. For MT's placement (opening the false-prophet unit): the add-nothing/take-nothing formula reads as a thematically apt motto for a chapter built entirely around temptations to add new gods or new signs to what is commanded, and ancient Near Eastern legal-collection convention places canon formulas at section boundaries in both directions. I do not find the WEB reading clearly superior to the MT reading on textual grounds alone -- the drafter's own low-confidence flag and explicit acknowledgment that this is 'a genuine cross-tradition seam, not a settled call' is the right posture, and I concur that this decision sits at a real interpretive frontier rather than being either confirmed or overturned by literary-form analysis.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: This is the book's named crux and I read it the way OL corrects it, not the way the frozen draft or LF's frontier_defer leaves it. Three facts check out exactly as claimed: a petuchah -- the heaviest divider Torah paragraphing offers -- sits after MT 13:1 with zero division anywhere between the setumah after 12:28 and that petuchah, so the manuscript delimits precisely MT 12:29-13:1 (=WEB 12:29-32) as one closed paragraph; the שְׁמֹר-frame closes 12:28 and then closes MT 13:1 too, a repeated closing device rather than an opening one; and MT 13:2 (כִּי יָקוּם בְּקִרְבְּךָ נָבִיא) is a fully self-sufficient casuistic opening needing no lead-in. The draft's own stated reason for its call -- that הַדָּבָר carries the article and therefore points backward -- does not survive comparison with 4:2, where the identical אֵת הַדָּבָר אֲשֶׁר אָנֹכִי מְצַוֶּה אֶתְכֶם construction is unmistakably prospective and uniformly plural (תֹסִפוּ, תִגְרְעוּ, both confirmed by direct inspection); the noun in both places is made definite by its own participial relative clause, not by pointing back to something already said. That argument needs retiring, but it is not load-bearing for OL's conclusion, which stands on the petuchah and the repeated frame instead. The one real counter-signal, absent from both the draft and LF's deferral, is the Numeruswechsel: 12:28-31 is 2ms throughout (verified: הִשָּׁמֶר לְךָ, תִּנָּקֵשׁ, תִּדְרֹשׁ, תַּעֲשֶׂה), MT 13:1 opens plural (אֶתְכֶם, תִשְׁמְרוּ) and closes singular (תֹסֵף, תִגְרַע), and MT 13:2 is singular again -- a genuine alternation, but one signal set against a petuchah plus a twice-used closing formula. On this record the seam is resolvable at candidate level rather than a true frontier: WEB 12:29-32 closing the centralization law is the better-corroborated reading, the plural head of MT 13:1 logged as a live counter-signal rather than a tie-breaker, and confidence should move from low to medium, not stay at frontier_defer.

primary_reviews.rationale: The chosen boundary (v.3 alone, split from v.4) is plausible, but the rejected-alternative analysis only tests the weaker of the two live alternatives. It rebuts merging v.3 forward into the land-animal register (v.4's narrower scope), but never considers the more natural alternative: merging v.3 backward with vv.1-2. All three verses share one unbroken theological ground -- v.1's “You are the children of Yahweh your God,” v.2's “For you are a holy people,” and v.3's “You shall not eat any abominable thing” read as a single holiness-preamble (identity claim, then two brief prohibitions flowing from it, mourning and food) before the specific positive register opens at v.4 with its own naming formula, “These are the animals which you may eat.” Unlike 12:1's אֵלֶּה-colophon, which is a grammatically marked heading device with book-wide precedent (1:1, 4:44), v.3 has no comparable heading marker -- its status as a standalone heading is inferred from topical breadth alone, which is a thinner basis than the drafter's own precedent citation implies. This does not mean the drafter's three-verse split (v.1-2 / v.3 / v.4-8) is wrong, only that the strongest competing reading -- a two-verse split at v.1-3 / v.4-8 -- was not engaged.

primary_reviews.rationale: I think the span is probably right, but the evidence offered for it does not survive checking, and the rating cannot stand. The rationale claims an inclusio 'repeated verbatim' in Hebrew: v.11 כָּל צִפּ֥וֹר טְהֹרָ֖ה תֹּאכֵֽלוּ and v.20 כָּל ע֥וֹף טָה֖וֹר תֹּאכֵֽלוּ. Those are not the same words — different noun (צִפּוֹר, feminine, versus עוֹף, masculine) and correspondingly different adjective. The repetition is verbatim in WEB's rendering only, which is exactly the kind of translation artefact an original-language pass exists to catch. peer_crosscheck.assessment: This is the range's central dispute, so I checked every Hebrew fact behind the out-of-band merge argument directly against the text. The ten-participle claim is accurate: מַקְלֶה (16), מַסִּיג (17), מַשְׁגֶּה (18), מַטֶּה (19), שֹׁכֵב four times (20, 21, 22, 23), מַכֶּה (24), לֹקֵחַ (25) - ten Qal or Hiphil participles, while only the frame verses use אֲשֶׁר-clauses: v.15's אֲשֶׁר יַעֲשֶׂה and v.26's אֲשֶׁר לֹא יָקִים. The response-formula claim is also accurate: v.15 alone carries the plural וְעָנוּ כָל הָעָם וְאָמְרוּ אָמֵן, while vv.16-26 repeat the identical four-word וְאָמַר כָּל הָעָם אָמֵן eleven times without variation, and every unit is exactly one verse. I also checked M8-Deut-187's own frozen rationale for 28:38-42: it does merge five items differing in named content (seed, vineyard, olive, children, trees) by calling them 'the identical futile-labor pattern' - so the internal-inconsistency charge against the campaign's application of its own register criterion is fair on its face. Having verified the facts, I still come down on upholding the twelve-way split, but not primarily on the 'distinct offense' ground the frozen rationale leans on, since that ground alone is genuinely in tension with the 28:38-42 merge. What actually distinguishes this series is a discourse-frame signal neither position foregrounds enough: every curse closes with its own discrete performative response, present without exception after all twelve, while 28:38-42 has no repeated closing formula at all and runs as one uninterrupted fronted-object clause chain. A performed unit closed by its own ritual response is a stronger and more consistent basis for one-verse granularity than offense-naming alone, and it simply does not apply to the agricultural-loss catalog. The two-witness file corroborates this reading unusually strongly for this campaign: OSHB records a samekh after every one of MT 27:15 through 27:25, and a petuchah - the strongest class - after 27:26, an unbroken run of independent section punctuation matching every one of the twelve proposed seams. That is weak-to-strong corroboration, not the basis for the ruling by itself, but its density here is exceptional and does support raising confidence. The three-part אֲשֶׁר-frame alternative (15 | 16-25 | 26) does not hold up under the same scrutiny: it would group ten curses naming ten different offenses into one bloc solely because they share a participle rather than a relative clause, ignoring that each of the ten already has its own complete Amen closure - a morphology-only argument the campaign's own symmetry rule would flag as insufficient standing alone. Recommendation: uphold the twelve-way split; revise the rationale to foreground the per-curse Amen closure as the primary signal rather than offense-naming alone; raise confidence from low to medium given the near-total two-witness corroboration.

primary_reviews.rationale: The rationale's central evidentiary claim — that v.27 opens “a fresh יַכְּכָה sub-wave” — does not hold up against the Hebrew text. The identical form יַכְּכָה יְהוָה already opens v.22, five verses earlier, and it sits inside the immediately preceding decision's own span (M8-Deut-182), whose own rationale explicitly lists יַכְּכָה as one member of a “sustained verb-chain (יַדְבֵּק, יַכְּכָה, יִתֵּן, יִתֶּנְךָ)” absorbed into one larger unit. The same word cannot simultaneously be just one interchangeable verb within a diverse chain at v.22 and the very marker of freshness that opens a new, separately-bounded unit five verses later at v.27 — that is an internal inconsistency in how the same formula is being weighted. If יַכְּכָה יְהוָה recurrence is the operative signal, the more consistent reading either treats the whole v.20-29 stretch as one continuous “Yahweh will [verb] you” catalog with this verb simply recurring inside it, or, if a seam is wanted at every occurrence, requires one at v.21/22 too, which the preceding decision does not draw. This does not necessarily mean the v.26/27 line itself is wrong — the specifically named skin, eye, and mind ailments of vv.27-29 do form a recognizable sub-group distinguishable from the plague/weather/defeat catalog of vv.20-26 — but the stated evidence for calling v.27's opening “fresh” is inaccurate as written.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: Both challenges are correct and reinforce each other. I traced every occurrence of יַכְּכָה יְהוָה in the chapter directly against the text: MT 28:22 (inside M8-Deut-182's own span, explicitly listed there as one member of a diverse verb chain), MT 28:27 (opening this decision), MT 28:28 (one verse later, still inside this very decision's own span, and not treated as opening anything further), and MT 28:35 (opening the next decision). That is two internal occurrences, not one, inside spans that never treat the verb as an opener - which makes the 'fresh sub-wave' framing for v.27 self-contradicting on the campaign's own terms: the identical form is simultaneously ordinary chain vocabulary at 22 and 28, and the sole warrant for a new unit at 27. Neither challenge asserts the boundary itself is wrong, and that's the right posture - the skin, eye, and mind ailments named in vv.27-29 (שְׁחִין ... גָּרָב ... שִׁגָּעוֹן ... עִוָּרוֹן ... תִּמְהוֹן לֵבָב) are a recognizable content sub-group distinguishable from the weather-and-defeat imagery of vv.20-26. But the stated evidence for the seam needs to change: drop the verb-recurrence claim, falsified by v.28's own presence inside the same span, and ground the cut in the ailment-content shift instead, or accept that the more consistent reading merges this decision back into M8-Deut-182 as one unbroken 28:20-29 catalog, since no independent formula, marker, or addressee change exists at the 26/27 line.

The decisive difference from the Ebal curses is structural, not lexical: this span has no repeated closing formula and no discrete response after each item - one uninterrupted syntactic run, where the curses are twelve separately closed performances. I'd recommend tightening this rationale's language to the כִּי-clause register rather than 'identical pattern,' since as worded it supplies exactly the ammunition the twelve-curse internal-consistency objection uses against the campaign.

primary_reviews.rationale: I affirm this decision on the strength of its opening. וְהָיָה כִי + protasis is one of the most reliable onset formulas in the book, it stands at a chapter head, and a setumah closes the material before it. The closing edge is a different question and I have lodged my objection against the decision that owns it rather than duplicating it here — see M8-Deut-201. Should that challenge be sustained, this span absorbs 30:7-10 and runs to the petuchah after MT 30:10.

Tested against the actual text, this decision's endpoint at v.6 does not correspond to any marked seam. WEB places no paragraph break between v.6 and v.7, and the whole span from v.1 through v.10 is a single extended promise built on one recurring phrase: "return to Yahweh your God and obey his voice... with all your heart and with all your soul" (v.2), echoed at v.8 ("You shall return and obey Yahweh's voice") and again at v.10 ("if you obey Yahweh your God's voice... if you turn to Yahweh your God with all your heart and with all your soul"). That three-fold refrain brackets the whole unit, and the cascading "Yahweh your God will..." verb chain (release, v.3; bring, v.5; circumcise, v.6; put, v.7; make prosperous, v.9) runs uninterrupted across the proposed seam at v.6/7. WEB's only paragraph break in this stretch falls between v.10 and v.11, exactly where the next decision correctly begins.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: The span itself is fine -- command, grounding clause, and purpose stay inside one instruction closing before v.22's fulfillment report -- but boundary_evidence_refs[1] is not a citation slip, it is an altered word. It labels 'oshb:Deut.31.21' the string כִּי אֵדַע אֶת יִצְרוֹ אֲשֶׁר הוּא עֹשֶׂה הַיּוֹם, and checking Deut_oshb.txt directly, MT 31:21 reads כִּי יָדַעְתִּי אֶת יִצְרוֹ אֲשֶׁר הוּא עֹשֶׂה הַיּוֹם. אֵדַע (a 1cs imperfect, 'I will know') does not occur in the verse; the actual form is יָדַעְתִּי, a qatal ('I have known'/'I know'). That is not a trivial variant -- the verse's whole logic is that Yahweh already knows the people's inclination before the conquest, which the imperfect would undercut. Given the same class of defect turned up twice already in this range as reference-number slips, this one is worse: it is a fabricated verbal form inside quotation marks presented as verbatim.

primary_reviews.rationale: My objection is to the stated reason rather than to the grouping in the abstract. The rationale defends the merger on the ground that the two verses sit 'within the same "same day" temporal frame with no fresh formula separating them'. Both halves of that are wrong on the text. בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא occurs in v.22 only and does not extend over v.23; and v.23 opens וַיְצַו … וַיֹּאמֶר, a waw-consecutive with a new addressee introduced — formally the same kind of onset the draft treats as decisive at 31:7 (וַיִּקְרָא מֹשֶׁה לִיהוֹשֻׁעַ) and at 31:16. The WEB layout separates the two verses. MT offers no mark either way, and absence is not counter-evidence, so this does not rise to a certain over-merge; but a merger justified by a formula that is present and a time-frame that is not cannot stand as written.

primary_reviews.rationale: The literature_type_guess ("song_composed_and_joshua_recommissioned") treats v.22 and v.23 as one register, a narrator's report of same-day compliance, but v.23's content does not fit that description. "He commissioned Joshua the son of Nun, and said, Be strong and courageous... for you shall bring the children of Israel into the land which I swore to them. I will be with you" uses first-person divine-oath language ("I swore," "I will be with you") that belongs to Yahweh, not Moses; Moses never swears the land to Israel anywhere in this book, only Yahweh does. Read this way, v.23 is very likely Yahweh's own direct commissioning of Joshua, resuming the purpose clause stated back at v.14 ("Call Joshua... that I may commission him"), with v.22's report of Moses's song-writing functioning as a parenthetical aside between two moments of the same Tent-of-Meeting scene rather than its continuation.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: The rationale's two factual props both fail on inspection. בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא ('that day') is present in v.22's own clause and nowhere in v.23 -- checking Deut_oshb.txt, v.23 has no temporal phrase at all, so the 'same temporal frame' claim doesn't hold. And v.23 does open with a fresh formula, וַיְצַו...וַיֹּאמֶר, structurally the same command-plus-speech pairing this book uses elsewhere to mark a new address (compare 31:7's וַיִּקְרָא...וַיֹּאמֶר to Joshua). Separately, the content point LF raises is worth weighing on its own textual merits, not as theology: v.23's אֶהְיֶה עִמָּךְ ('I will be with you') and אֲשֶׁר נִשְׁבַּעְתִּי לָהֶם ('which I swore to them') echo v.21's אֲשֶׁר נִשְׁבָּעְתִּי almost verbatim, both first-person oath language Yahweh uses of himself elsewhere in this chapter and that Moses does not use of himself anywhere in the book. Whether or not the campaign resolves who speaks v.23, grouping it with v.22 as uniform third-person narrator report is not defensible once the fresh formula and the absent 'same day' frame are accounted for.

primary_reviews.rationale: The central empirical claim -- that a full sweep of every וַיְצַו in Deuteronomy shows four instances (27:1, 27:11, 31:10, 31:25) continuing with לֵאמֹר and 31:23 alone not -- was independently re-run against the whole book text, not just the row's own citations: a direct search of Deut_oshb.txt for the standalone form וַיְצַו turns up exactly these five occurrences and no others (וַיְצַוֵּנוּ at 6:24 is a distinct inflected form with a pronominal object suffix and is correctly not counted among them). The claim is therefore exhaustively verified, not merely illustrated. The distinction drawn from 31:7's וַיִּקְרָ֨א מֹשֶׁ֜ה...וַיֹּ֨אמֶר אֵלָ֜יו (a different introducing verb, call-plus-speech) versus 31:23's command-plus-speech pairing is grammatically accurate on inspection. The oath-language parallel to v.21 was independently checked: 31:21 ends אֶל הָאָ֖רֶץ אֲשֶׁ֥ר נִשְׁבָּֽעְתִּי, matching אֲשֶׁ֣ר נִשְׁבַּ֣עְתִּי לָהֶ֑ם in v.23 closely, supporting the speaker-is-Yahweh reading, which is also the standard critical reading of this crux. Medium confidence is a defensible call given that speaker attribution in unmarked biblical narration is inherently interpretive even when the grammatical case is strong. Tiling against M8-Deut-210 (31:22) and M8-Deut-211 (31:24-31:29, opening on an unrelated fresh temporal clause about the law-book's deposit) is clean. The strongest rejected alternative -- v.23 as Moses's own continued narrated action alongside v.22 -- is the genuine prior reading and is engaged and answered on its own grammatical terms, not dismissed by assertion.

primary_reviews.rationale: וַיְהִי כְּכַלּוֹת is a temporal-macro-syntactic opener, one of the strongest onset devices available in narrative Hebrew, and it is doing real work here: it marks the completion of the prose scroll as distinct from the song just composed. The draft's insistence on the different object — book rather than song — is right and is what keeps this from collapsing into the preceding decision. Closing on הַקְהִילוּ is likewise a genuine imperative turn.

This decision's endpoint at v.27 falls in the middle of one uninterrupted quotation. "Moses commanded the Levites... saying" opens at v.25, and the quotation does not close until the end of v.29 ("to provoke him to anger through the work of your hands."); v.26's ark-deposit instruction, v.27's rebellion rationale, v.28's elders-summons, and v.29's corruption prediction are all inside that single quoted command with no reintroducing formula anywhere in between. WEB places no paragraph break at v.27/28 at all -- the only paragraph break in this stretch of text falls between v.29 and v.30, exactly where the quotation closes and third-person narration resumes.

primary_reviews.rationale: The Song's opening edge is secure — a petuchah and the הַאֲזִינוּ vocative together. The internal close at 3|4 has no formal support and the draft says so plainly, which I credit. I accept it nonetheless because the turn is clean rather than intrusive: v.3 ends a first-person invocation with an imperative to ascribe greatness, and v.4 begins a verbless predication on a new subject (הַצּוּר תָּמִים פָּעֳלוֹ). No syntactic chain is severed. That is the distinction I have applied throughout — a content-only cut is tolerable at a clean clause juncture and not tolerable mid-chain.

The genre shift here is doubly marked: WEB's own q1/q2 poetic lineation begins precisely at v.1, and the addressee shifts from heaven-and-earth-as-witness (vv.1-3) to Israel-as-accused (v.4 onward) exactly where this decision draws its line. A formal typesetting cue and a content cue converge on the same seam, unusually strong support for a boundary in this book.

primary_reviews.rationale: This is the most serious defect I found. The rationale defends the span by claiming that between the vengeance declaration and the taunt against the foreign gods 'no |b marker separates them'. There is one, and it falls after v.35. I confirmed it in the raw file: the sequence reads \v 35 … 'Their doom rushes at them.' then \b then \q1 \v 36 'For Yahweh will judge his people'. The chapter carries six blank-line markers in total — after vv. 22, 27, 33, 35, 38 and 42 — and the draft's cluster-28 scheme uses five of them while denying the existence of the sixth, which happens to be the one that falls inside this span. Compounding it, the alternative the draft considers and rejects is drawn at 36|37, not at the marker's actual position. And the Hebrew independently confirms a turn at 35|36: vv.34-35 are Yahweh's first-person reservation of vengeance (לִי נָקָם וְשִׁלֵּם), while v.36 switches to third-person predication about Yahweh (כִּי יָדִין יְהוָה עַמּוֹ) and introduces the quoted taunt. So the boundary the draft's own criterion demands is also the one the source language supports.

Worth recording that MT itself does not divide after this verse — the Masoretic paragraph runs 33:1-6 — so the isolation of the heading rests on the mode shift rather than on a mark, which is legitimate since text signals drive and absence is not counter-evidence.

Verse 1 is pure third-person narration about Moses ("This is the blessing with which Moses the man of God blessed the children of Israel before his death"), while v.2 pivots into quoted poetry marked by both "He said," and the onset of q1/q2 lineation, a doubled formal signal, introducing formula plus genre shift, for treating the superscription as its own unit.

I do not propose relocating the boundary — the shift to per-tribe address is real — but the evidence must be restated to what the text actually supports.
